entries.modern_form: PIE *h₂enǵʰ- 'to constrict, tighten; narrow, painfully constricted' (Pokorny angh- 42–43; Watkins/AHD angh- 'tight, painfully constricted, painful')
entries.note: Root form, language label and gloss are all right. Pokorny IEW 42–43 heads the entry 'angh- (kelt. auch engh-) ‚eng, einengen, schnüren‘, z. T. auch von seelischer Beklemmung, Angst' and lists exactly the branches Nourai draws (Avestan verbal forms, Latin ango/angustus, Germanic angr/angust); AHD gives 'angh-. Tight, painfully constricted, painful ... [Pok. ang̑h- 42.]'. Two cross-cutting caveats: (1) the Avestan form printed in the book, 'azaehě', is not a real Avestan word — the PDF page image confirms the book itself prints 'azaehě', so this is Nourai's own corruption (not a scan error) of Av. ǫzaŋhē (Bartholomae AiW 363–4, Pokorny p.42 'ǫzaŋhē'); (2) the ni-āz / niyāz branch is claimed by a different root in current Iranian scholarship: Cheung, Etymological Dictionary of the Iranian Verb (2007) 171–172, files Av. niiāzata / niiāzaiiən and MP/Pth./Sogd./NP niyāz under *Haz 'to drive, lead' (PIE *h₂eǵ-, Skt. aj-, Lat. agō), not under *angh-. Bartholomae, Walde-Pokorny I 62 and Moʼin (following Bartholomae) all support Nourai; Cheung is the dissent.

ref_check.note: POK_01.txt ↵-leaf 50 (printed p.42/43 — the '43' page numeral falls inside this leaf): 'anghos-, anghes ‚Beklemmung, Bedrängnis‘: ai. ámhas- n. ‚Angst, Bedrängnis, Not‘ ..., av. ǫzah- ‚Bedrängung, Not, Gefangenschaft‘ ... lat. angor m. ... angus-tus ‚eng‘ (aus *anghos-to-s); angustiae'; the database text POK_full.txt gives 'Root / lemma: angh- (*hengh-) / Meaning: "narrow, *press" ... References: WP. I. 62 f., WH. I 47. / Page(s): 42-43'. Grep: grep -n 'lemma: angh-' POK_full.txt.

nodes.derivation: Two items. (a) 'azaehě' is a corrupt rendering of Young Avestan ǫzaŋhē, the infinitive of ǫz- 'to lace up, constrict, oppress' (Bartholomae AiW s.v.: 'j. ǫzaŋhe Inf. ‚zu bedrängen, in Not zu bringen‘: avaŋhe narǫm ašaonǫm ǫz° Yt 13.39'), beside the s-stem ǫzah- n. '1) Ein-, Zusammenschnürung der Kehle, Erdrosselung; 2) Bedrängung, Enge, Not; Gefangenschaft' (Yt 10.22, V 16.10, Y 10.17). Phonology: PIE *h₂enǵʰ- > Proto-Iranian *anź- > Av. ǫz- (the nasal is written with the nasalised vowel ǫ before the fricative), the exact match of Lat. angō/angor and Skt. áṃhas-. So Nourai's gloss 'compressed, in need' is right and the arrow root→Avestan is right for this word, but the printed shape is impossible Avestan. (b) 'ni-az' = Av. ǫz- with the preverb ni-, in the lengthened grade *ni-āz-, attested only in finite forms: ni-āzata 'she laces her waist in' (Yt 5.127, of Anāhitā) and ni-āzaiiən 'they shall wedge (it) in' (V 13.30). No Avestan noun *ni-āz- 'need' exists — Nourai's gloss 'that which pushes you down, need' back-projects the Middle Persian abstract. Walde-Pokorny I 62 print exactly this set ('Verbal av. ǫzaŋhe ‚zu bedrängen, in Not zu bringen‘, tiefstufig av. ny-azata ‚sie schnürt sich‘, ny-āzayən ‚sie sollen hineinzwängen‘'), and Bartholomae's own footnote to ǫz- points forward to 'np. niyāz ‚Mangel‘ bei Hbm. AGr. I.105'. THE DISPUTE: Cheung 2007:171–172 removes ni-āz from this root altogether and files it under Proto-Iranian *Haz 'to drive, lead' (< PIE *h₂eǵ-, Skt. aj-, Lat. agō), reading YAv. caus. (+ni-) 'to straiten' (citing De Vaan 2003:34), with MP nydʾc /niyāz/, Pth. nyʼz, Sogd. nyʼz and NP niyāz listed as its nominal continuations. Because the node's second word is assigned to a different root by the current standard work, the node takes the worse verdict.

ref_check.note: POK_full.txt s.v. angh-: 'Material: Verbal: Avestan ǫzaŋhē “to press”, lengthened grade Avestan ny-azata “she squeezes herself into her corset”, ny-azayen “to wedge oneself in” ... Page(s): 42-43'; the German original (POK_01.txt leaf 50) has 'av. ǫzah- ‚Bedrängung, Not, Gefangenschaft‘'. So p.42 does carry both of Nourai's Avestan items — but in the shapes ǫzaŋhē / ny-āzata, not 'azaehě'.

MIDDLE PERSIAN: (+ *ni-) BMP nydʾc /niyaz/, MMP nyʼz ‚want, need, misery’ ... NWIR: (+ *ni-) NP niyaz ‚need’.' Cheung thus takes the very forms Pokorny/Bartholomae use as *angh- evidence and assigns them to PIE *h₂eǵ- 'drive' instead.

nodes.derivation: Middle Persian niyāz, Book Pahlavi ⟨nydʾc⟩ = ⟨nyʾc⟩, Manichaean MP and Parthian ⟨nyʼz⟩ 'need, want, misery' (MacKenzie, Concise Pahlavi Dictionary s.v.), with the derivatives niyāzōmand 'needy' and niyāzōmandīh 'poverty' and the negated compound abē-niyāz 'free from want'. Formally it is an Old Iranian action-noun *ni-āza- built to the verb seen in Av. ni-āz-: the preverb ni- + ā of the lengthened grade gives MP niyā- (the glide y is automatic between i and ā), and Old Iranian intervocalic -z- is kept, spelt ⟨c⟩ in Book Pahlavi. Age: Armenian took the compound over in the Arsacid period as apeṛniaz / apeniaz 'without need' = MP abē-niyāz (Hübschmann, Persische Studien §91), which shows the word already existed in Middle Iranian; Sogdian nyʼz 'need' and Christian Sogdian nyʼzʼwt 'needy' show the same formation in the eastern branch. Only the ultimate root attribution is contested (see node 1); that MP niyāz contains ni- + the āz- verb is agreed by everyone, Cheung included.

nodes.derivation: MP niyāz passes into New Persian unchanged as نیاز niyāz 'need, want', with the derived adjectives نیازمند / نیازومند niyāz(ō)mand 'needy' (= MP niyāzōmand) — exactly the two forms Nourai prints in the box — and the Islamic-era religious sense 'votive offering made to obtain a wish' (Moʼin sense 2; Farhang-e Neẓām, quoted in Moʼin's note to Borhān). The second word نیازی niyāzī 'beloved, sweetheart' is a separate lexicographic item: Asadi Ṭusi's Loghat-e Fors already has «نیاز، دوست بود» with Labībī's line «ایا نیاز بمن ساز و مر مرا مگذار», and Rashīdī corrects him: «لیکن بمعنی دوست، نیازی است نه نیاز» — i.e. in the 'friend/beloved' sense the correct form carries the -ī, which is why Nourai's chart gives 'nîâzî: need, dear friend, sweetheart'; the ʿOsmān Mokhtārī couplet he quotes (دلم خستهٔ ناز توست ای نیازی) uses it in that sense. Semantically the 'sweetheart' sense is the object of one's niyāz, i.e. 'the one one longs for'.

nodes.derivation: An empty pass-through box standing for the Latin branch of *h₂enǵʰ-: the verb angō, -ere 'to press tight, throttle; to distress' (the exact match of Gk. ἄγχω and Av. ǫzaŋhē), its nouns angor 'constriction of the throat; anguish' and angina 'quinsy', the adjective anxius (< *angh-s-io-) 'uneasy, solicitous', and the s-stem adjective angustus < *angh-os-to-s 'narrow' with its abstract angustia(e) 'narrowness, straits, distress'. Ernout–Meillet stress that the double sense Nourai needs is Latin-internal: 'Ango se dit du physique et du moral; ce même double sens se retrouve dans les substantifs dérivés'. Both English words in the daughter box come out of this Latin material.

nodes.derivation: Two different routes out of the Latin box. ANXIOUS is a learned 16th/17th-c. borrowing straight from Latin anxius 'solicitous, uneasy' (formed to angere), with English -ous substituted for Latin -us; the noun anxiety likewise from anxietas, -atis. ANGUISH came by the popular route: Latin angustia (classical plural angustiae) 'narrowness, straits' > Old French anguisse, angoisse 'choking sensation, distress, anxiety, rage' (12th c., Modern French angoisse) > Middle English anguise, angoise (c.1200), whence the verb anguish from OF anguissier, angoissier. The semantic path is 'tightness/choking' > 'straits, difficulty' > 'mental torment'.

nodes.derivation: An empty pass-through box for the Germanic branch of *h₂enǵʰ-. The adjective *angwuz 'narrow' (Goth. aggwus, ON ǫngr, OE enge, OS engi, OHG angi/engī, G. eng) continues *anghu-; the s-stem *angaz- (< *anghos-, the same formation as Skt. áṃhas- and Lat. angor) gives ON angr 'grief, affliction'; and *angusti- (< *anghos-ti-, revocalised after *anghu-) gives OHG angust, OFris. angost, German Angst. Nourai's box leads only to English anger, i.e. to the ON angr reflex.

nodes.derivation: Not a native English word: Middle English angre (n., mid-13c., first 'distress, suffering, affliction'; v. c.1200 'to vex, irritate') is a loan from Old Norse angr 'grief, sorrow, affliction' / angra 'to grieve, vex' taken over in the Danelaw — the same Norse layer as e.g. ill, skin, take. The Proto-Germanic base is *angaz < *anghos-. The modern sense arose by transfer from the injury to the feeling it provokes ('the expression was transferred to the feelings of resentment naturally aroused in the mind of the person aggrieved'), giving 'rage, wrath' by the early 14th c., whence angry.

entries.note: The root box itself is right: Pokorny 43–45 heads 'angʷ(h)i- ‚Schlange, Wurm‘' and AHD 'angʷhi-. Snake, eel.' What Nourai's single box hides is the split Pokorny states in his own first line: 'egʷhi-, ogʷhi- und eghi- ds.; mindestens zwei etymologisch verschiedene, aber früh verschränkte Sippen, deren Verhältnisse noch vielfach unklar sind.' Current handbooks separate *h₂éngʷʰis (Lat. anguis, Lith. angis, OPruss. angis, OCS *ǫzь, Pol. wąż) from *h₁ógʷʰis / *h₃égʷʰis (Skt. áhi-, Av. aži-, Gk. ὄφις, Arm. iž), which is where the Avestan branch of this chart actually belongs (see node 1). Ernout–Meillet put it bluntly: 'Le flottement porte sur l'initiale: e-, o-, an-, et sur les consonnes *gʷ, *gʰ, *gʷʰ ... On ne peut donc restituer un original indo-européen.' Separately, Walde–Pokorny I 65 reject the once-popular idea that *angʷ(h)is 'snake' is a 'constrictor' derived from the neighbouring root angh- 'to press' — 'ist wegen der Gutturalverschiedenheit und sachlich zu bestreiten' — which matters because Nourai prints Angh and Angwhi side by side on this page.

Lat. anguis = lit. angis (f.), apr. angis ‚Schlange‘ ...'; POK_full.txt: 'Root / lemma: angʷ(h)i- ... Meaning: “snake, worm, *fish” ... Page(s): 43-45.'

nodes.derivation: Both words are real. Av. aži- (stem ažay-) m. is 'snake' and, by extension, 'dragon, monster' — Bartholomae AiW: 'j. ažay- m. 1) ‚Schlange‘, ein daēvic animal (V 18.65, V 14.5) ... 2) schlangenähnliches Untier ‚Drache, Ungeheuer‘ (Y 9.30 ažiš sairitaʾ, Aog. 78)'; it is the exact cognate of Skt. áhi-, Gk. ὄφις, Arm. iž, Lat. anguis. aži.dahāka- is the three-headed serpent-tyrant of Yt 5.29–35, Yt 9.14, Yt 19.37 and Y 9.8, killed by Θraētaōna; Nourai's shape 'aži-dahâkô' is the Avestan nominative singular ažiš dahākō, the very form used by Horn (Grundriss no. 76 'aw. ažiš dahākō') and Hübschmann ('zd. aži dahākō'). WHY ONLY 'plausible': the arrow from the root box as drawn is phonologically wrong under the modern reconstruction. Av. aži- goes back to Proto-Iranian *Háǰiš < Proto-Indo-Iranian *Háǰʰiš < *h₁ógʷʰis — the NASAL-LESS variant. Pokorny himself puts it there, not under the nasal form: on printed p.44 he writes 'gr. ὄφις ‚Schlange‘ (*ogʷhis): cymr. euod (*ogʷh-): ai. ahi-, av. azi- ‚Schlange‘', i.e. in the *ogʷhi- paragraph, while Latin anguis heads the *angʷhi- paragraph. Klein hedges the same way ('prob. also with OI. ahiḥ, Avestic azish'), and Buck notes the two sets come 'fr. parallel forms with and without nasal, but phonetic relations in part obscure'. So the family relationship is real and old, but 'Avestan aži derives from *angʷhi-' is not what modern sources say. Nourai's gloss 'biting snake' for aži-dahāka- is also only one of several proposals for dahāka-, whose meaning is unsettled (variously 'stinging/harming', 'man-like', or a reflex of the ethnonym Dahā/Dahae).

ref_check.note: POK_01.txt leaf 52 (printed p.44, the '45' numeral follows a few lines later): 'gr. ὄφις ‚Schlange‘ (*ogʷhis): cymr. euod (*ogʷh-): ai. ahi-, av. azi- ‚Schlange‘.' The page cited does carry Av. azi- — exactly as Nourai claims — but under the *ogʷhi- variant, not the nasal one.

Klein does say precisely this, s.v. anguine: 'L. anguinus, fr. anguis, ‚serpent, snake’, which is cogn. with Arm. auj, oj, Lith. angis, OPruss. angis, Lett. uodze, Russ. už, Pol. wąż, and prob. also with OI. ahiḥ, Avestic azish, ‚snake’, Gk. ἔχις, ‚viper’', and s.v. Ahi: 'OI. ahiḥ, ‚serpent’, rel. to Avestic azish and cogn. with Gk. ἔχις, L. anguis'. But the page number does not match the copy on disk: in KLN_1966.txt the anguine/anguish entries sit in ↵-leaf 53, whose printed numerals read 77–79 (the calibration leaf = floor(p/2)+12 would put p.86 at leaf 55–58, which is the anth-/anti- material, containing no snake entry). nodes.derivation: Old Iranian aži-dahāka- > Middle Persian až(i)dahāg (Book Pahlavi ʿcydhʿk', Manichaean MP ʿzdhʿg) > New Persian اژدها aždahā, by the regular loss of final MP -g and of the intervocalic stop; the fuller اژدهاک eždehāk preserves the -k and, in Borhān, is glossed as the last sense of اژدها, i.e. ضحاک ماران (Moʼin's footnote: 'مخفف اژی‌دهاک، ضحاک'). Horn (no.76) shows the date: the Armenian loan aždahak proves that the Middle Persian pronunciation was already až-, not aǰ-, in Arsacid/Sasanian times. The Semitic round-trip Nourai marks with ضحّاک in the box is real and runs Persian > Arabic > Persian: Asbaghi (PLA 190) has Arabic ضحّاک ḍaḥḥāk, folk-etymologised as the Arabic active participle 'the laugher / name of a king', from Persian aždahā 'Drache' < aži-dahāka > Pazand Dahāk 'evil, demonic king', 'arabisiert in ẓaḥḥāk'; and PLA 5 has a second, unassimilated Arabic borrowing أزدهاق azdahāq 'a particular dragon' straight from Persian. اژدر aždar is the shortened Persian form, from which Turkish ejder/ejderha and Bulgarian/Serbian ažder were taken (PLA 190); Borhān glosses اژدر as 'مار بزرگ ... و سر علم و رایت'. The modern military sense 'torpedo' (اژدر دریایی) is a 20th-c. Persian coinage on the dragon image, not an old sense. Nourai's extra gloss 'also a spear' for eždehā is Ferdowsi's metaphor and is exactly what Noushin's Shāhnāma glossary records.

nodes.derivation: Latin anguis (m., f. in early Latin) 'snake' is the direct reflex of the nasal form *h₂éngʷʰis and is exactly superposable on Lith. angis, OPruss. angis, Latv. uodze, OCS *ǫzь, Pol. wąż, Russ. už. It is an old religious/poetic word, largely replaced in prose by serpēns and uīpera (Pliny has it 40× against 360× serpēns); its derivatives are anguinus, anguiculus, and the diminutive-shaped anguilla 'eel' (paralleled by OPruss. angurgis, Lith. ungurys, Pol. węgorz for the same 'snake-fish' idea). It is the only word in this chart that the modern reconstruction actually assigns to *angʷʰi-.

nodes.derivation: A learned borrowing, not an inherited word: English anguine 'snakelike, pertaining to a serpent' (17th c.) is Latin anguinus, the adjective of anguis, with the Latin -inus ending anglicised as -ine; the parallel anguineous renders anguineus. No French intermediary is needed, and the word has stayed a bookish one. AHD gives ANGUINE (with ANGUILLIFORM) as the English yield of this root through Latin.
